name: Imagination inflation
statement: Imagining a childhood event that probably did not happen raises a person's confidence that it did, by a small amount.
meaning: The procedure has three steps. People rate how sure they are that each of a list of childhood events happened to them, on a scale running from definitely did not happen to definitely did happen. Some weeks later they imagine a few of those events in guided detail, while the rest go unimagined and serve as controls. They then rate the whole list again. Confidence rises more for the imagined events than for the control ones, and that gap is the effect. The claim is about belief rather than recollection. Garry and her colleagues have argued that inflation is a shift in how likely an event seems, not an implanted memory with imagery and a narrative attached. Ratings usually stay in the lower half of the scale afterwards, so Mazzoni and Smeets and their co-authors describe the shift as reducing the belief that an event did not happen rather than building a belief that it did. The forensic interest is in what happens when police or therapists ask somebody to picture an episode they cannot recall.

origin.who: Maryanne Garry, Charles G. Manning, Elizabeth F. Loftus and Steven J. Sherman
origin.note: The paper coined the term and built the Life Events Inventory procedure the field still uses. It borrowed the idea from work on future events, where Carroll had shown in 1978 that imagining an election result raised belief in it.

evidence: Garry and colleagues pretested 46 students at the University of Washington on a 40-item Life Events Inventory, and 38 finished the study. Each item asked how certain they were that an event had happened before the age of 10, from 1, definitely did not happen, to 8, definitely did happen. Eight items were targets, split into two subsets of four. Two weeks later each person imagined one subset in guided steps lasting about two minutes an item, while the other subset went unimagined. The experimenter then claimed the original forms had been misplaced and handed out a second copy. Analysis was confined to items first rated 1 to 4, which was 76% of the responses and gave 112 imagined and 119 not-imagined items. Most ratings did not move, 57% in the imagined condition and 65% in the control. Confidence rose for 34% of imagined items against 25% of control items. A paired t test treating the eight events as cases put the gap at 8.2 percentage points, t(7) = 5.48, p = .0009. Jumps straight to 8 were rare, six of the 112 imagined items and two of the 119 controls, and removing them left a gap of 6.55 points, t(7) = 3.02, p = .01. On the broken window item, 24% of those who imagined it grew more confident against 12% of those who did not. Heaps and Nash repeated the design at the University of Tennessee with 55 students and a fresh event list. The item-level gap came to 8.1 percentage points, t(7) = 1.94, p < .047, one-tailed. Averaging within people instead of within events, confidence rose 0.44 scale points for imagined events and 0.18 for controls, t(54) = -1.89, p < .032, one-tailed. Hypnotic suggestibility, r = .35, and dissociativity, r = .34, predicted who inflated, while imagery vividness and interrogative suggestibility did not. Goff and Roediger ran a version with actions rather than childhood events. Forty-four Rice University undergraduates took part and 40 entered the analysis of the first experiment. They heard simple statements such as break the toothpick, and performed, imagined or merely heard each one. In a second session they imagined some actions once, three times or five times. At test they judged whether each action had been heard, imagined or performed in the first session. Claiming to have performed an action that was never mentioned in the first session rose from .02 at zero imaginings to .04, .07 and .13 at one, three and five, F(3, 117) = 8.81, with a linear trend, F(1, 39) = 15.93.

replication.headline: Imagining moves confidence and the move is small: in 13 of the 14 datasets with usable means, the gain over not imagining was one point or less on an eight-point scale, and ratings stayed in the lower half.
replication.detail: Brewin and Andrews assembled 19 imagination inflation datasets on childhood events. Seventeen reported a test built on participants' own mean scores, and 11 of those found a significant difference between imagined and control events while six did not. Sharman and Barnier are the outlier in their table, with imagined events climbing from 1.86 to 5.50 and from 2.02 to 5.54 for negatively and positively valenced events, against control rises from 1.82 to 3.72 and from 1.97 to 4.19. Dudek and Polczyk ran a registered report with 279 participants and found the main effect, with confidence rising 0.74 points for imagined items and 0.18 for controls, Wald chi-squared(1) = 23.43, p < .001. Their own hypotheses, that people who distrust their memories inflate more, were not supported, with Bayes factors of .132 and .153 favouring the null. The standing challenge is regression to the mean. Pezdek and Eddy reproduced the design with 43 younger and 32 older adults and argued the whole effect is that artifact. The surface pattern matched: for items first rated 1 to 4, ratings rose for 39% of imagined and 25% of control items. Items first rated 5 to 8 fell instead, in both conditions, and so did non-target items, which is what regression predicts. An analysis of variance found no interaction between test occasion and imagination condition, F(1, 73) = 0.78, and for each of the four target events the residuals against a regression line fitted to the control condition did not differ from zero. Their own item-level analysis, the one Garry used, went the other way and gave a 14.2-point gap favouring imagination, t(3) = 2.65, p < .05, wider than Garry's 8.2. Garry, Sharman, Wade, Hunt and Smith replied in the same issue that residualised change scores cannot detect an effect that lifts every score by the same amount, and that Pezdek and Eddy had confused the mean of the items with the midpoint of the scale. Brewin and Andrews, who are sceptical of this literature, tested the regression account by inspecting the control groups. Among the nine datasets with a significant effect and usable group means, the control change was positive in five cases and negative in four, which they read as evidence that regression contributes little.

study.cite: Dudek, I., & Polczyk, R. (2025). Memory distrust and imagination inflation: A registered report. PLOS One, 20(8), e0327638.

limits: This entry covers imagination inflation for autobiographical childhood events, along with Goff and Roediger's action-event version. It does not cover the misinformation effect, memory implantation through a relative's testimony or a doctored photograph, or false feedback about childhood food, all of which use different procedures and return different numbers. The search ran across Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, PLOS and the open web on 10 August 2026 and located no meta-analysis of imagination inflation. Brewin and Andrews give a reason one would be of limited value, which is that the studies too rarely measure the same moderator variables. Their review is the source here for the tally of 19 datasets, for the count of significant tests, and for the Sharman and Barnier figures, none of which were read in the original papers. The other studies in their table, including Paddock's, Horselenberg's, Mazzoni and Memon's and Bays', were also not read here. The structured effect-size fields are left empty on purpose. The 1996 paper reports a gap in percentage points between events and the later work reports scale points between people, and those two quantities are not comparable. Almost every dataset in the literature is drawn from university students, and Brewin and Andrews note that only four of the 61 studies in their wider review included older adults. Nothing here bears on implausible or traumatic events, because the Life Events Inventory is built from mundane ones.
misreadings: Imagination inflation is read as memory implantation, and its own authors say it is not. Garry, Sharman, Wade, Hunt and Smith wrote that the effect is a rise in confidence that a hypothetical event was experienced, and that it fails the conditions other researchers set for an implanted memory. They quote Mazzoni's point that people are confident their births happened as their mothers describe them without remembering the birth. The published effect sizes for one and the same test disagree. Garry and colleagues printed 0.72 for the 1996 result, using the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the not-imagined items. Five years later the same first author printed 1.94 for the same t test using Cohen's formula, and flagged the change in a footnote. Heaps and Nash printed 0.68 for the item-level version of their own result and 0.44 for the person-level version. Any single number quoted for this effect is quoting one of those choices. Regression to the mean is offered as a debunking and does not do that work. Target events are picked because people rate them low, so their ratings drift upward on a second test whether or not anyone imagines them. That drift is what the control items measure, and the effect is the difference between the two conditions. Garry and colleagues raised the possibility themselves in 1996, and Pezdek and Eddy's own low-rated items showed a 14.2-point gap in favour of imagination. The proportion of items whose rating moved is also quoted as a rate of false memory. In Garry's data the most common outcome by a wide margin was no change, and jumps to the top of the scale happened six times in 112 imagined items.
